content: In the comparison group, decisions regarding infant feeding were primarily influenced by the involvement of the male partner and the socioeconomic status of the mother. To promote adherence to optimal infant feeding practices, it is recommended to involve male partners, family members, and the broader community in providing support. Self-reported data may introduce bias. A study by Bland in 2008 demonstrated that lay counselors were effective in promoting and sustaining exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) among both HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. Community-wide promotion of EBF, rather than targeting only HIV-positive women, is essential. EBF has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of breastfeeding-associated HIV transmission. Educational and counseling interventions were strongly associated with higher EBF rates, particularly when combined with access to antiretroviral therapy during antenatal and postnatal periods. Group education, when paired with individualized counseling and frequent contact during antenatal and postnatal care, has been shown to improve EBF rates. Educational programs should focus on basic HIV facts and safer breastfeeding practices. Increased frequency of contact with healthcare providers was associated with improved EBF adherence. Promoting EBF can reduce postnatal HIV transmission among women unaware of their HIV status and should be supported by child survival and HIV prevention programs. The introduction of therapeutic education and counseling during antenatal and postnatal care, along with access to antiretroviral therapy, positively impacted EBF rates. Community health worker interventions nearly doubled EBF rates, with each additional visit increasing EBF adherence by 6%. Home visiting models were found to be both feasible and effective. However, data stratification by HIV status was not performed in some studies, which may introduce bias. To improve EBF adherence, it is necessary to involve family members, particularly fathers, in infant feeding counseling and education. Targeting less-educated mothers with intensive counseling and appropriate methods, educating on the benefits of EBF, and providing guidance on milk production are critical. Encouraging regular attendance at antenatal and postnatal care is also essential. Recall bias may affect the reliability of self-reported data. Exclusive breastfeeding initiation among HIV-positive mothers significantly increased following postnatal care interventions. High-quality, integrated prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs and maternal and newborn health (MNH) services are feasible and acceptable. These programs promote early postnatal visits and improve care for both HIV-positive and HIV-negative mothers and their infants. Despite improvements, breastfeeding practices among HIV-positive women still fall short of national and international recommendations. Cost-effective strategies are needed to enhance breastfeeding practices in this population. The overall transmission rate of HIV was relatively low, suggesting the effectiveness of antiretroviral prophylaxis. However, further efforts are required to address gaps in adherence and education. In summary, effective interventions to support breastfeeding among HIV-positive women include community health worker visits, group education, individualized counseling, and access to antiretroviral therapy. These strategies improve EBF rates, reduce HIV transmission, and enhance maternal and child health outcomes.
